title: Leaving out to-infinitives
subtitle: I won't be able to / I forgot (to)
summary: Shorten a to-infinitive clause to just to, leave it out altogether, or keep to be after the verb be.

lesson.heading: to instead of the whole clause
lesson.text: When the context makes the meaning clear, we can use to on its own instead of a whole clause beginning with a to-infinitive.

examples.text: I wanted to come with you, but I won't be able **to**.
examples.note: instead of ... to come with you

examples.text: It might have been better if Rosa had asked for my help, but she chose not **to**.

lesson.heading: After be, repeat to be
lesson.text: If the verb in the previous clause is be, the to-infinitive form to be is repeated in the next clause.

examples.text: Leon was frightened - or maybe he just pretended **to be**.
Dan has lost a lot of weight. He's much thinner than he **used to be**.

lesson.heading: Is to optional or necessary?

left.label: to can be included or left out
left.text: After most nouns and adjectives that take a to-infinitive, and after verbs like agree, ask, begin, forget, promise, refuse, start, try.
examples: I'm not going to write another book - at least I don't have any **plans (to)**.
*A:* Could you and Tom help me move house? *B:* Well, I'm **willing (to)**, and I'll ask Tom.
Alex will collect us by 10 o'clock. He **promised (to)**.
*A:* You were supposed to buy some sugar. *B:* Sorry, I **forgot (to)**.

right.label: to must stay
right.text: After verbs that need a complement to finish their meaning.
examples: I admit that I took her watch, but I didn't **mean to**.
Have you thought about getting vaccinated against cholera before going there? I'd certainly **advise you to**.

lesson.note: Optional to: also chance, idea, opportunity, promise, suggestion; afraid, delighted, determined. to must stay after: afford, be able, choose, deserve, expect, fail, hate, hope, intend, love, need, prefer.

lesson.heading: want and would like in if- and wh-clauses
lesson.text: After want and would like in an if-clause or a wh-clause we can often either leave the to-infinitive out or use to.

examples.text: You're welcome to dance if you'd **like (to)**.
You can do whatever you would **like (to)**.
Come and see us when you **want (to)**.

lesson.heading: In other clauses, keep to
lesson.text: If the clause is not an if-clause or a wh-clause, to is included.

examples.text: I was planning to see you tomorrow, and I would still **like to**.
I offered to clean your car because I really **want to**, not because I hope to be paid.

lesson.heading: if you like or if you'd like (to)?

left.label: *like* - no to
examples: You can have one if you **like**.

right.label: *'d like (to)*
examples: You can have one if you'd **like (to)**.

lesson.heading: Negatives always keep to
lesson.text: With negative forms of want, would like and like, to is included - even in if- and wh-clauses.

examples.text: *A:* Shall we go and visit Laura? *B:* I don't really **want to**.
I should have phoned Jo last night, but it was so late when I got home I didn't **like to**.
*A:* He won't mind you asking him for a loan. *B:* Oh, no, I wouldn't **like to**.

lesson.text: Don't stop at to when the first clause used be: '... or maybe he just pretended to be', not ~~pretended to~~.

exercises.prompt: She occupies a much less important role in the company than she ___.
exercises.explanation: To stands for the whole clause 'to occupy an important role'.

exercises.prompt: Dan has lost a lot of weight. He's much thinner than he ___.
exercises.explanation: The verb being replaced is be, so we repeat to be.

exercises.prompt: Lucia was frightened - or maybe she just ___.
exercises.explanation: After be in the first clause we keep to be.

exercises.prompt: Luka had to admit that he'd failed, even though he obviously ___.
exercises.explanation: Hate needs a complement, so to cannot be left out.

exercises.prompt: Spain won 3-0, and ___, after a fine performance.
exercises.explanation: Deserve is another verb that must keep to.

exercises.prompt: The Pantheon in Rome wasn't anything like I ___.
exercises.explanation: Expect keeps to, and because the verb replaced is be we add be as well.

exercises.statement: *A:* Will Sara be able to play? *B:* I asked her, but she says she doesn't want.
exercises.explanation: ... she doesn't want to. Negative forms of want always keep to.

exercises.statement: *A:* Can the children come too? *B:* Yes, of course, if they want.
exercises.explanation: Correct. In an if-clause, to after want can be left out (... if they want to is also fine).

exercises.prompt: *A:* Shall we go out walking tomorrow? *B:* Yes, ___ very much.
exercises.explanation: This is not an if- or wh-clause, so to must be included.

exercises.statement: *A:* Could I ask you a personal question? *B:* Of course. Ask anything you like to.
exercises.explanation: Ask anything you like. (or ... you'd like to.) In a wh-clause we usually leave out to after like.

exercises.prompt: Explain why you offered to clean the car, keeping to at the end of the middle clause.
exercises.answer: I offered to clean your car because I really want to, not because I hope to be paid.
exercises.explanation: This is not an if- or wh-clause, so want keeps to.

exercises.prompt: Must to be included, or can it be left out?

items.text: I don't have to walk to work. I do it because I choose ...
*A:* Would you like to travel first class? *B:* Well, yes, I'd certainly prefer ...
I was hoping to go to Russia this year, but I can't afford ...
When the police officer told the crowd to leave the square they refused ...
We didn't want Alina to leave college, but she was determined ...
*A:* Would you present the prizes for the competition? *B:* I'd be delighted ...
*A:* Shall we ask Dad before we borrow the car? *B:* Yes, it might be a good idea ...
